{{Primary sources|article|date=July 2011}}

'''Bernard Leonard Cohen''' (June 14, 1924 – March 17, 2012) was [[Professor Emeritus]] of [[Physics]] at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. Cohen, who was born in [[Pittsburgh]],<ref name="phyast.pitt.edu">{{cite web |first=Bernard L. |last=Cohen |title=Resume |url=http://www.phyast.pitt.edu/~blc/Vita-Pub.htm |publisher=University of Pittsburgh |access-date=23 March 2011}}</ref><!--SPS exception: about self--> was a staunch opponent of the so-called [[linear no-threshold model]] (LNT) which postulates there exists no safe threshold for radiation exposure. His view has support from a minority.<ref>{{cite journal |pages=125–36 |doi=10.1016/j.taap.2004.02.007 |title=Hormesis: from marginalization to mainstream: A case for hormesis as the default dose-response model in risk assessment |year=2004 |last1=Calabrese |first1=E |journal=[[Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology]] |volume=197 |issue=2 |pmid=15163548 |bibcode=2004ToxAP.197..125C }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| first=Jerome S. | last=Puskin | title=Letter to the Editor: Reply to Cohen's Response to EPA Position on Cancer Risk from Low Level Radiation | journal=Dose-Response | year=2010 | volume=8 | issue=3 | pages=387–388 | pmc=2939694 | pmid=20877494 |doi=10.2203/dose-response.10-012.puskin}}</ref> He died in March 2012.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/postgazette/obituary.aspx?n=bernard-l-cohen&pid=156579866&fhid=4365 |title=BERNARD L. COHEN Obituary: View BERNARD COHEN's Obituary by Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |publisher=Legacy.com |date= |accessdate=2012-03-20}}</ref>

==No-threshold and plutonium toxicity debates==
Cohen claimed: "All estimates of the cancer risk from low level radiation are based on the [[linear-no threshold theory]] (LNT) which is based solely on largely discredited concepts of radiation [[carcinogenesis]], with no experimental verification in the low dose region of the most important applications. These risk estimates are now leading to the expenditure of tens of billions of dollars to protect against dangers whose existence is highly questionable. It is therefore of utmost importance to test the validity of this theory."<ref>{{cite book |title=Standard Handbook of Environmental Science, Health, and Technology |editor-first=J. H. |editor-last=Lehr |publisher=[[McGraw-Hill]] |location=New York |year=2000 |chapter=Introduction and Chapter 20.2 |isbn=978-0-07-038309-8}}</ref>{{verify inline|reason=Is this really citing both the introduction and a chapter, or is it the introduction to the chapter?|date=October 2026}}

A conclusion, with an update to the landmark study published 1995, continues:

{{quote|
Since no other plausible explanation has been found after years of effort by myself and others, I conclude that the most plausible explanation for our discrepancy is that the linear-no threshold theory fails, grossly over-estimating the cancer risk in the low dose, low dose rate region. There are no other data capable of testing the theory in that region.

An easy answer to the credibility of this conclusion would be for someone to suggest a potential not implausible explanation based on some selected variables. I (or he) will then calculate what values of those variables are required to explain our discrepancy. We can then make a judgement on the plausibility of that explanation. To show that this procedure is not unreasonable, I offer to provide a not-implausible explanation for any finding of any other published ecological study. This alone demonstrates that our work is very different from any other ecological study, and therefore deserves separate consideration.<ref name="ConclusionStandard">{{cite book |title=Standard Handbook of Environmental Science, Health, and Technology |editor-first=J. H. |editor-last=Lehr |publisher=[[McGraw-Hill]] |location=New York |year=2000 |chapter=Conclusion |isbn=978-0-07-038309-8}}{{Page needed|date=July 2011}}</ref>}}

Cohen's debates in academic periodicals and published correspondence with [[R. William Field]], [[Brian J. Smith]] (assistant professor of [[biostatistics]], [[University of Iowa]]), [[Jerry Puskin]] (from the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|U.S. Environmental Protection Agency]]), [[Sarah Darby]], and Sir [[Richard Doll]] and others regarding his radon-related ecologic studies are well known.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://radlab.nl/radsafe/archives/0202/msg00329.html |title=Cohen's fallacy |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927041759/http://radlab.nl/radsafe/archives/0202/msg00329.html |archive-date=September 27, 2007 |publisher=University of Iowa}} Published correspondence.</ref>{{dead link|fix-attempted=yes<!--Archive URL is invalid!-->|date=October 2026}}<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.ovid.com/jnls/health-physics/abstract/00004032-199807000-00004~response-to-criticisms-of-smith-et-al |title=Response to Criticisms of Smith et al. |first=Cohen |last=Bernard L. |journal=Health Physics |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=23–28 |date=July 1998}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Allison |first=Wade |year=2009 |title=Radiation and Reason: The Impact of Science on a Culture of Fear |location=York, England |publisher=York Publishing Services |page=2 |isbn=0-9562756-1-3}}</ref> Among other expert panels, the [[World Health Organization]]'s [[International Agency for Research on Cancer]] discussed at length Cohen's results then concluded: "The weight of evidence is that the ecological analyses of Cohen can be rejected."<ref>{{cite book |series=IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans |volume=78 |title=Ionizing Radiation |chapter=Part 2: Some Internally Deposited Radionuclides |publisher=World Health Organization, International Agency for Research on Cancer |year=2001 |url=http://monographs.iarc.fr/ENG/Monographs/vol78/mono78.pdf |isbn=9789283212782}}</ref>

In March, 2011, Professor Cohen stated, reflecting on his study and its controversial results, that low levels of radiation can have beneficial health effects and reduce the risks of cancer:

{{quote|There is evidence on both sides. Whether low-level radiation is protective against cancer, a theory called [[radiation hormesis]], is debated in the scientific community. Furthermore, ... [on his viewpoint, and its support found in his exhaustive studies] it could go further and say that no confounding factors (like socio-economic, geography, ethnicity, medical care access, and beyond 500 explored in the analysis) can explain the results. However, my study was designed to test the assumption that the danger of radiation is simply proportional to the radiation dose, which is the only evidence that low-level radiation may be harmful. My conclusion was that that assumption is false.<ref name="phyast.pitt.edu"/><ref name="ConclusionStandard" /><ref>Referring to comments on the topic by [[Ann Coulter]]:
* {{cite news |title=Claim of radiation benefits barely passes X-ray test for truth |date=March 23, 2011 |newspaper=[[The Oregonian]] |page=A2 |location=Portland, Oregon}}
* {{cite web |url=https://politifact.com/factchecks/2011/mar/22/ann-coulter/ann-coulter-says-lexposure-low-levels-radiation-ar/ |first=Robert |last=Farley |date=March 22, 2011 |title=Ann Coulter says exposure to low levels of radiation is good for you, reduces cancer risk |website=[[PolitiFact]] |access-date=8 October 2026}}</ref>}}

Other scientists disagree<ref>{{cite journal |pages=141–148 |doi=10.1088/0952-4746/22/2/302 |title=The potential for bias in Cohen's ecological analysis of lung cancer and residential radon |year=2002 |last1=Lubin |first1=Jay H. |journal=Journal of Radiological Protection |volume=22 |issue=2 |article-number=302 |pmid=12148789|bibcode = 2002JRP....22..141L |s2cid=250890569 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |pages=599–631 |doi=10.1080/15287390500260960 |pmid=16608829 |title=An Overview of the North American Residential Radon and Lung Cancer Case-Control Studies |year=2006 |last1=William Field |first1=R. |last2=Krewski |first2=Daniel |last3=Lubin |first3=Jay |last4=Zielinski |first4=Jan |last5=Alavanja |first5=Michael |last6=Catalan |first6=Vanessa |last7=Klotz |first7=Judith |last8=Létourneau |first8=Ernest |last9=Lynch |first9=Charles |last10=Lyon |first10=Joseph L. |last11=Sandler |first11=Dale P. |last12=Schoenberg |first12=Janet B. |last13=Steck |first13=Daniel J. |last14=Stolwijk |first14=Jan A. |last15=Weinberg |first15=Clarice |last16=Wilcox |first16=Homer B. |journal=Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health Part A |volume=69 |issue=7–8|bibcode=2006JTEHA..69..599W |s2cid=25665833 |display-authors=8 }}</ref> and more research has been called for.<ref>Ultra-Low-Level Radiation Effects Summit. January 2006. ORION International Technologies, Inc. (ORION) and sponsored by the U.S. Department of Energy's Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP) 3 April 2008.</ref>{{nonspecific|reason=Are there published proceedings? If so, which paper? If not, this is [[WP:V|unverifiable]] and so not an acceptable source|date=October 2026}}

Subsequent research would join a profound array of positions including a 1982 [[United Nations]]' work-group study – [[UNSCEAR]] – concluding: "There appear to be no nonspecific effects from low doses of radiation that result in a shortening of the life span."<ref>{{cite web |title=Appendix A: Radiation Safety Reference Manual |publisher=Vanderbilt University |page=19 |url=http://www.safety.vanderbilt.edu/pdf/appendix.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101214112703/http://www.safety.vanderbilt.edu/pdf/appendix.pdf |archivedate=2010-12-14 |access-date=26 March 2011}}</ref>{{verification failed|reason=Does not contain this sentence. Additionally this is apparently Appendix A of some larger work, but it's not clear what. There is a more recent Radiation Safety Manual that isn't marked "Appendix A" at https://www.vumc.org/safety/sites/vumc.org.safety/files/public_files/rad/radiation-safety-reference-manual.pdf  but it also doesn't contain this sentence|date=October 2026}}

==Scholarly achievements==
Professor Cohen earned his undergraduate degree from [[Case-Western Reserve University]] in 1944, his master's degree from the [[University of Pittsburgh]] in 1947, and his Ph.D. from [[Carnegie-Mellon University]] in 1950. He taught at the [[University of Pittsburgh]] from 1958 as Professor of Physics, Adjunct Professor of Chemistry, Adjunct Professor of Chemical and Petroleum Engineering, Adjunct Professor of Radiation Health at the Graduate School of Public Health; there also as Adjunct Professor of Environmental and Occupational Health. He was awarded professor emeritus standing in 1994.<ref name="phyast.pitt.edu"/>

From 1965 to 1978, he was Director of the [[Scaife Nuclear Laboratory]].{{citation needed|date=February 2020}}

A testimony to his conviction on the human safety of background low-level radiation was his offering rewards of up to $10,000 if people provided evidence that the inverse association he found between [[radon]] (county averages) and [[lung cancer]] (county averages) was due to some factor other than failure of the linear-no threshold theory. Puskin, Smith, Field and others have claimed that his findings are due in part to his inability to control for the inverse association between smoking and radon.<ref>{{cite journal |pages=526–532 |doi=10.1097/00004032-200304000-00012 |date=April 2003 |first=J. S. |last=Puskin |title=Smoking as a confounder in ecologic correlations of cancer mortality rates with average county radon levels |journal=Health Physics |volume=84 |issue=4 |pmid=12705451|bibcode=2003HeaPh..84..526P |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1234792 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |journal=[[Health Physics]] |date=February 2004 |last=Cohen |first=B. L. |url=https://www.ovid.com/jnls/health-physics/abstract/00004032-200402000-00013~the-puskin-observation-on-smoking-as-a-confounder-in |title=The Puskin observation on smoking as a confounder in ecologic correlations of cancer mortality rates with average county radon levels |volume=86 |issue=2 |pages=203–204}}</ref><ref>{{cite mailing list |mailing-list=Radsafe |first=Gary |last=Howard |date=14 June 2003 |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050127004231/http://www.vanderbilt.edu/radsafe/0306/msg00282.html |title=A respectable end to radon debate needed |publisher=Vanderbilt University}}</ref><!--relevance: this email thread includes emails from Cohen-->

When [[Ralph Nader]] described [[plutonium]] as "[[Plutonium#Precautions|the most toxic substance known to mankind]]", Cohen, then a tenured professor, offered to consume on camera as much [[Plutonium#Compounds|plutonium oxide]] as Nader could consume of [[caffeine]],<ref>{{cite book |first=Bernard L. |last=Cohen |title=Nuclear Energy |editor1-first=Karl Otto |editor1-last=Ott |editor2-first=Bernard I. |editor2-last=Spinrad |location=New York |publisher=Plenum Press |year=1985 |pages=355–365}}</ref>{{page needed|reason=It doesn't seem like he wrote the whole book. A search for this title and first editor suggests Ott as author, not editor. Also the title appears to be incomplete, it should probably be "Nuclear Energy: A Sensible Alternative"|date=October 2026}} the stimulant found in coffee and other beverages, which in its pure form has an oral median lethal dose ({{LD50}}) of 192&nbsp;milligrams per kilogram in rats.<ref name=ld50>{{cite journal | title = Factors Affecting Caffeine Toxicity: A Review of the Literature | last = Peters | first = Josef M. | journal = The Journal of Clinical Pharmacology and the Journal of New Drugs | volume = 7 | year = 1967 | issue = 3 | pages = 131–141 | url = http://jcp.sagepub.com/cgi/reprint/7/3/131 | accessdate = 2008-03-29 | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080610131732/http://jcp.sagepub.com/cgi/reprint/7/3/131 | archivedate = 2008-06-10 | doi = 10.1002/j.1552-4604.1967.tb00034.x | url-access = subscription }}</ref>  Nader did not accept the challenge.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/obituaries/2012/03/29/Obituary-Bernard-L-Cohen-Noted-physicist-and-Pitt-professor-never-wanted-to-stop-learning/stories/201203290300|title=Obituary: Bernard L. Cohen / Noted physicist and Pitt professor never wanted to stop learning|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |access-date=August 8, 2015}}</ref>

==Publications==
Professor Cohen has written six books, including ''Heart of the Atom'' (1967) with translations in French, German, Italian, and Japanese, ''Concepts of Nuclear Physics'' (1970) with translation in Arabic, ''Nuclear Science and Society'' (1974), ''Before It's Too Late: A Scientist's Case for Nuclear Power'' (1983), and ''The Nuclear Energy Option, Alternative for the Nineties'', (1990) in translation for Japanese and Spanish. He has written about 135&nbsp;research papers on basic [[nuclear physics]], about 300&nbsp;scientific papers on energy and environment (e.g. [[nuclear power]], health effects of [[radiation]], [[radioactive waste]], risks in our society), and about 80&nbsp;articles in popular magazines such as ''[[Physics and Society]]'', ''[[National Review]]'', ''[[Oui (magazine)|Oui]]'', ''[[Science Digest]]'', ''[[Catholic Digest]]'', and ''[[Scientific American]]''. He has authored scientific studies and editorial contributions on a vast array of subjects in nuclear industry trade journals such as ''[[Public Utilities Fortnightly]]'', ''[[Reviews of Modern Physics]]'', ''[[Nuclear Engineering International]]'', and ''[[American Journal of Physics]]''.<ref name="phyast.pitt.edu"/>

==Awards and honors==
Dr. Cohen received in 1981 the [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics]] from the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/bonner.cfm |title=Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics |publisher=[[American Physical Society]] |accessdate={{Format date|2011|4|11}}}}</ref> He was also elected Chairman of the [[American Physical Society]], Division of Nuclear Physics (1974–75).

Dr. Cohen received the 1992 [[Distinguished Scientific Achievement Award]] from the [[Health Physics Society]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://hps.org/aboutthesociety/people/awardlist.html |title=Health Physics Society Awards |publisher=Health Physics Society |accessdate={{Format date|2011|4|11}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://hps.org/aboutthesociety/people/dsarecipients.html |title=List of Distinguished Scientific Achievement Award Recipients |publisher=Health Physics Society |accessdate={{Format date|2011|4|11}}}}</ref> and the 1996 [[Walter H. Zinn Award]] from the [[American Nuclear Society]] (ANS), for his "notable and sustained contribution to the nuclear power industry that has not been widely recognized."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ans.org/honors/va-zinn |title=Walter H. Zinn Award |website=Honors and Awards |publisher=[[American Nuclear Society]] |accessdate={{Format date|2011|3|28}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Walter H. Zinn Award recipients |url=http://www.ans.org/honors/recipients/va-zinn |website=Honors and Awards, Recipients |publisher=[[American Nuclear Society]] |accessdate={{Format date|2011|3|28}}}}</ref> The ANS also granted Cohen its 1985 "Public Information Award",<ref name="phyast.pitt.edu"/>{{Better source needed|reason=I don't find this award listed on the ANS website or any other reference??|date=March 2011}} and its 1996 "Special Award", for his "meritorious contributions in research" on ''Linear Dose Model [Versus] Other Models for Critical Dose Values''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Special Award |url=http://www.ans.org/honors/va-special |website=Honors and Awards |publisher=[[American Nuclear Society]] |accessdate={{Format date|2011|3|28}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Special Award recipients |url=http://www.ans.org/honors/recipients/va-special |website=Honors and Awards, Recipients |publisher=[[American Nuclear Society]] |accessdate={{Format date|2011|3|27}}}}</ref> He was elected to member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2003,<ref name="NAE">{{cite web|url=http://www.nae.edu/MembersSection/Directory20412/30755.aspx |title=NAE Members Directory - Dr. Bernard L. Cohen |publisher=[[National Academy of Engineering|NAE]] |accessdate={{Format date|2011|4|7}}}}</ref> "for fundamental contributions to our understanding of low-level radiation" and Chairman of the [[American Nuclear Society]] Division of Environmental Sciences (1980–81).
